stories.headline: Lula wins a fourth term in Brazil's tight runoff
body: Brazil's 80-year-old president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won Sunday's runoff with about 51.8% of the vote.
His rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who led the first round, got about 48.2% and says he will ask courts to cancel the result.
Lula is the first candidate since 1989 to win after losing the first round, and he starts his new term on 5 January.
stories.joke: Most polls said Flávio, voters said Lula. Pollsters may want a recount of their own careers.
stories.vc: Brazil is Latin America's biggest market. A disputed result can shake its currency and stocks, while a calm handover would steady investors in its fintech and farm-tech scene.

stories.headline: Venezuela's opposition leader Machado comes home to cheering crowds
body: Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina Machado returned to Venezuela on Sunday after more than 10 months in exile.
Crowds waving flags surrounded her car, and more supporters packed the roads into the capital, Caracas.
She returns to a country reshaped by the US, which removed Nicolás Maduro in January and has run talks without her.
stories.joke: Ten months away, and still the most popular person at a party she wasn't invited to.
stories.vc: Venezuela has some of the world's biggest oil reserves. A clear path to elections would open the door to energy and infrastructure money; more doubt keeps it shut.

stories.headline: Israel locks down the West Bank before Tuesday's vote
body: Prime Minister Netanyahu ordered a closure of Hebron and a full lockdown of the West Bank after an attack at a checkpoint on Friday.
Two Israeli soldiers and the two gunmen were killed, and several people were wounded.
The order came days before Israelis vote on Tuesday, in an election where polls show no clear winner.
stories.vc: Security shocks and a close election can keep Israel's markets jumpy this week. Investors in Israeli tech will watch who can form a government.

stories.headline: Indian shares fall four days in a row as oil nears $114
body: India's stock market fell for a fourth straight day on Friday, with the Nifty 50 closing at 22,600.
The Nifty lost 2.4% over the week as Brent crude oil climbed close to $114 a barrel.
Costly oil raises worries about inflation, the rupee and company profits, and the market opened lower again on Monday.
stories.joke: Crude at $114 is the only thing in your portfolio that's up this week.
stories.vc: When oil spikes, Indian stocks get cheaper but company margins get squeezed. Favour businesses that can pass on costs, and keep some cash for better prices.

stories.headline: Jio Platforms shares are allotted today, listing on Wednesday
body: Share allotment for the ₹30,213 crore Jio Platforms IPO is due today, 26 October.
The shares are set to list on the NSE and BSE on Wednesday, 28 October; the top of the price band was ₹1,119.
Unofficial grey-market trading points to a premium of about 22%, but that is no promise of the listing price.
stories.joke: Half of India applied. The other half is waiting to say 'I told you so' on listing day.
stories.vc: A strong Jio debut could pull more big Indian companies to list at home. Watch whether the listing pop holds after day one.

stories.statLabel: Q2 profit, from a ₹154 cr loss
stories.headline: Bengaluru's Ather Energy turns profitable
body: Bengaluru-based electric scooter maker Ather Energy made a net profit of ₹1.3 crore in July to September.
In the same quarter a year earlier, it lost ₹154.1 crore.
The swing came in its Q2 results for this financial year.
stories.joke: An EV maker in profit. Somewhere a petrol scooter just stalled in shock.
stories.vc: A profit at Ather shows Indian EV makers can make the numbers work. That makes the EV supply chain, from batteries to chargers, easier to fund.

stories.headline: Unhedged: why Britain wants a boring budget
body: Britain's chancellor, John Healey, delivers the annual budget on Wednesday, 28 October.
The UK has the highest borrowing costs in the G7, so the interest bill on its debt is a big cost to control.
On the FT's Unhedged podcast, economics commentator Chris Giles explains why dull is good for public finances.
stories.joke: A finance minister promising to be boring: the rare pledge everyone hopes is kept.
stories.vc: When a government pays more to borrow, safe bonds compete harder with risky bets. High UK yields can pull money away from startups and growth stocks.

stories.headline: Anthropic files publicly for what could be a record IPO
body: Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, released its public IPO filing on Monday.
The listing, expected in mid-November, could value it at more than $2 trillion, above SpaceX's $2.1 trillion debut in June.
Revenue jumped to $16.3 billion in the six months to June, though it also reported big losses, mostly from an accounting charge.
stories.joke: Wall Street finally found an IPO that makes SpaceX's look modest.
stories.vc: A blockbuster AI listing would set the price tag for every AI company. Late-stage investors will use it to judge what the leaders are really worth.

stories.headline: Legal AI startup Legora raises $550M at $8.8B
body: Swedish legal AI company Legora raised $550 million at an $8.8 billion valuation, in a round led by Atreides Management.
Its yearly recurring revenue is now above $200 million, and it went from $1 million to $100 million in under 18 months.
Its biggest rival, Harvey, raised $550 million at a $15.5 billion valuation a month ago.
stories.joke: Lawyers bill by the hour. Legora bills by the unicorn.
stories.vc: Law is one of the first big professions where AI is clearly paying off. Watch for the same pattern in accounting, tax and compliance.

stories.headline: Stratechery takes its first sponsor: Stripe
body: Ben Thompson's Stratechery newsletter is now presented by Stripe, its first sponsor in 12 years.
Thompson calls himself the internet's number one fan of ads, yet he had never run any on Stratechery.
The deal starts with filmed episodes of his Sharp Tech podcast and a bonus subscriber episode every Sunday.
stories.joke: The internet's biggest fan of ads finally runs one. Only took 12 years.
stories.vc: Creator businesses can add sponsors without losing trust when the fit is right. One respected sponsor can beat many small ads.

stories.statLabel: Big Tech vs the rest of the S&P 500
stories.headline: Apollo economist: AI has paid off only for Big Tech
body: Apollo's chief economist, Torsten Slok, says AI has brought 'zero payoff' to big US companies outside tech so far.
For the S&P 500 minus the seven tech giants, revenue per worker and profit margins are flat.
He thinks the problem may last, though a New York Fed study found better gains for public firms overall.
stories.joke: AI wrote the strategy deck. Profits are still waiting their turn.
stories.vc: If AI gains stay with the tech giants, the winners are the toolmakers, not their customers. Back startups that show real profit gains for clients, not just demos.
